title: THE CHARACTER I ALMOST OVERLOOKED: ONESIMUS
paragraphs: THE CHARACTER I ALMOST OVERLOOKED: ONESIMUS
Some of the most powerful lessons in Scripture come from the people we almost miss.

Not the kings.
Not the prophets.
Not the miracle workers.
But the quiet names hidden in short letters.
One of those names is Onesimus.
His entire story appears in a single chapter of the New Testament — the letter of Philemon. No long biography. No dramatic speeches. Just a few lines.
But those few lines carry one of the most beautiful pictures of redemption in the Bible.
Onesimus was a runaway slave.
At some point he fled from his master, Philemon, who was a Christian living in Colossae. In Roman culture, a runaway slave could face severe punishment if caught.
Running away was dangerous.
Returning was even more dangerous.
Yet somehow, during his escape, Onesimus encountered the apostle Paul. At the time, Paul was in prison for preaching the gospel.
And there, in chains, Paul did something extraordinary.
He led Onesimus to Christ.
Paul writes in Philemon 1:10:
That line alone tells us something powerful.
The runaway slave became a spiritual son.
Grace had found him.
But the story does not end with Onesimus simply believing in Jesus and disappearing into a new life somewhere else.
Paul did something unexpected.
He sent Onesimus back.
Back to the very man he had run from.
Imagine the weight of that journey.

The dusty road.
The uncertainty.
The fear of what might happen when the door opens.
Onesimus was not returning as the same man.
He was returning changed.
Paul writes this remarkable line in Philemon 1:11:
"Formerly he was useless to you, but now he is indeed useful both to you and to me."
Even his name carried meaning.
The name Onesimus literally means useful or profitable.
But Paul admits something honest.
Once, he was not living up to that name.
Once, he was running.
Once, he was lost.
But grace rewrote his story.
And then Paul makes one of the most radical statements in the letter.
He tells Philemon to receive Onesimus no longer as a slave, but more than a slave — as a beloved brother (Philemon 1:16).
Think about how revolutionary that was in the Roman world.
The gospel did not simply forgive Onesimus.
It transformed his identity.
The runaway became family.
The slave became a brother.
The man who once ran from responsibility now walked back toward it — carrying a letter from an apostle and a changed heart.
That is what real transformation looks like.
Many people want forgiveness without change.
Many people want grace without accountability.
Many people want a new beginning that never requires them to face what they left behind.
But Onesimus teaches us something deeper.
Sometimes the evidence of real transformation is the courage to return differently.
To go back with humility.
To go back with truth.
To go back not as the person you used to be — but as someone Christ has changed.
Onesimus could have stayed hidden.
He could have stayed in the safety of distance.
Instead, he walked back into the place where his past lived.
Why?
Because the gospel does not just change where we are going.
It changes who we are becoming.
And when Christ truly changes someone, the transformation becomes visible.
Paul believed in that transformation so much that he wrote these words to Philemon:

"If you consider me your partner, receive him as you would receive me."
— Philemon 1:17
That is astonishing.
Paul places Onesimus under the protection of the gospel.
In other words:
Treat him as you would treat me.
Grace had elevated the status of a runaway slave to the level of a beloved brother in Christ.
That is the power of redemption.
And here is the part that convicts me.
Onesimus is barely mentioned in Scripture.
Yet his story has echoed through history for two thousand years.
Because sometimes the people we overlook carry the lessons we most need.
Your past may explain your story.
But it does not have the authority to define your future.
Grace can rewrite identities.
Runaways can become brothers.
Broken people can become useful again.
And the places you once ran from may one day become the places where redemption is most visible.
Onesimus reminds us that the gospel is not just about escaping judgment.
It is about becoming someone new.
Someone humble.
Someone faithful.
Someone willing to walk back into difficult places with a changed heart.
A runaway slave walked up to a door with a letter in his hand.
But heaven saw something different.
Not a fugitive.
A brother.
And sometimes the characters we almost overlook end up teaching the greatest lessons of all.
What do you think took more courage for Onesimus — running away, or coming back changed?
